title: Galvanic and Electrolytic Cells
seo_title: Year 12 Chemistry: Electrochemical Cells Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Galvanic cells: anode, cathode, salt bridge and electron flow; standard electrode potentials and the electrochemical series; calculating cell e.m.f.; electrolytic cells and electrolysis; batteries, rechargeable cells and fuel cells. (Senior Secondary Chemistry, Unit 3: Equilibrium, acids and redox reactions)
meta_desc: Free Year 12 Chemistry worksheets on electrochemistry: galvanic cells, salt bridges, standard electrode potentials, cell e.m.f., electrolysis, batteries and fuel cells. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: AN OX, RED CAT: oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode.
body_html:
How to think about it

In a galvanic cell a spontaneous redox reaction makes electricity: oxidation at the anode (negative), reduction at the cathode (positive), electrons through the wire and ions through the salt bridge. The half-cell with the more positive E° is the cathode.

An electrolytic cell uses electricity to drive a non-spontaneous reaction; here the anode is positive. Rechargeable batteries act as galvanic cells when discharging and electrolytic cells when charging. Fuel cells run on a supply of fuel such as hydrogen.

Example

Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V and Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V. E°cell?

cathode Cu, anode Zn

0.34 − (−0.76)

Answer: 1.10 V

Example

Which electrode is negative in that cell?

Zn is oxidised

Answer: the zinc anode

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the anode is always positive: it is negative in a galvanic cell.
  • Saying electrons move through the salt bridge.
  • Subtracting the E° values the wrong way round.

faq.q: What is the difference between a galvanic and an electrolytic cell?
faq.a: A galvanic cell turns chemical energy into electrical energy with a spontaneous reaction; an electrolytic cell uses electrical energy to force a non-spontaneous reaction.

faq.q: Why are hydrogen fuel cells described as clean?
faq.a: The only product is water. But the hydrogen must be made cleanly, for example by electrolysis using solar or wind power.

items.q: A cell is made from the Zn²⁺/Zn (E° = −0.760 V) and 2H⁺/H₂ (E° = 0 V) half-cells. Which half-cell is the negative electrode?
items.e: The more negative E° is the negative electrode, where oxidation happens.

items.q: A cell is made from the Fe²⁺/Fe (E° = −0.440 V) and 2H⁺/H₂ (E° = 0 V) half-cells. Which half-cell is the negative electrode?

items.q: What is the job of a salt bridge?

items.q: Calculate the standard e.m.f. of a cell made from the I₂/2I⁻ (E° = 0.540 V) and Br₂/2Br⁻ (E° = 1.09 V) half-cells.
items.e: E°cell = E°(more positive) − E°(more negative) = 1.09 − (0.540) = 0.550 V.

items.q: What is the standard hydrogen electrode?

items.e: All E° values are measured against it.

items.q: What does the half-equation Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu represent?

items.q: How is the e.m.f. of a standard cell calculated?
c: E°cell = E°(reduction half, cathode) − E°(oxidation half, anode)
items.e: A positive E°cell means the reaction is spontaneous.

items.e: A reaction is feasible when the oxidising agent's E° is more positive than the reducing agent's (E°<sub>cell</sub> > 0).
